name: Place Bellecour
label: Place Bellecour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Bellecour' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Bellecour' (relation/2196752): middle (394 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4161405: 'Statue équestre de Louis XIV', the best-known feature inside 'Place Bellecour' (395 m across).
notes: One of Europe's largest open squares, with the Louis XIV statue.

text.description:
Place Bellecour is the great open square at the heart of Lyon, and it is the easiest place in the city to get a clean, wide photo. It measures 312 m by 200 m, with no trees or flowerbeds, so nothing gets in the way. The surface is a warm red, and the building façades around the edge make a tidy frame. In the middle stands the equestrian statue of Louis XIV, put up in 1825 and made by François-Frédéric Lemot. An earlier statue of the king from 1713 was destroyed during the Revolution in 1793. At the west end there is a second statue, of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry with the Little Prince, added in 2000.

The classic picture puts the statue in the foreground, with the Fourvière basilica rising on its hill behind. A tighter or wider lens changes how much square and how much basilica you get, so try more than one. If you want the whole sweep of the square against the façades instead, turn and shoot across the open space. In winter a Ferris wheel and an ice rink may appear in your frame, which can be fun or a nuisance depending on what you want.
text.geographic_location: Place Bellecour is in the 2nd arrondissement, in the middle of the Presqu'île between the Saône and the Rhône, just north of the Ainay district. Vieux Lyon and the cathedral face it across the Saône.
text.directions_text: The square is at the centre of Lyon's Presqu'île, so it is easy to find on the map from almost anywhere in the centre. From further out, the square has its own metro station, Bellecour (lines A and D), and is also served by buses including 10, 14 and 88. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with Fourvière behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole open square and the line of façades. Telephoto (2x-3x, if your phone has it) pulls the basilica closer to the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Bellecour (around the equestrian statue of Louis XIV at the centre, framing Fourvière hill behind it). The square's red surface and the Louis XIV statue in the foreground, with the Fourvière basilica rising on the hill behind. From here you see the red surface of the square and the Louis XIV statue in the foreground, with the Fourvière basilica on the hill behind. For a different view, the Jardin des Curiosités gives a high view over the city with Place Bellecour below; check the official site for access before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the basilica in the upper part of the frame. Crouch slightly so the statue stands out against the sky rather than against the buildings. Keep the phone level so the façades stay straight. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or let a few stay for a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the basilica keep their detail. Take a few frames at 0.5x, 1x and 2x and compare them later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The light direction matters here, so look at where the sun is on the day. If the sun is behind the basilica, try moving a few steps to one side to avoid glare.

text.access_note: Place Bellecour is an open pedestrian square, but events and seasonal fittings such as the ice rink can take up part of it, so check the official site before you go if you need a clear view.
claims_not_in_sources: The Fourvière basilica is seen to the west or north-west when looking from the centre of the square towards the statue.
Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people on the square.
If the sun is behind the basilica, glare can be a problem and moving to one side helps.
The square is open to the public at all times of day.
The Jardin des Curiosités is an elevated viewpoint over the city whose access arrangements should be checked in advance.

name: Parc de la Tête d'Or
label: Tête d'Or Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Île du Souvenir' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Île du Souvenir' (way/8134041): middle (157 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4077207: large area 'Parc de la Tête d'Or' (1765 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Huge city park with a lake, rose garden and greenhouses.

text.description:
Parc de la Tête d'Or is the largest urban park in Lyon, at about 117 hectares, and it sits in the north of the 6th arrondissement. It opened in 1857 on former Rhône floodplain, laid out by the Swiss designers Bühler. The lake is its most recognisable scene, and that is where this spot is set. The park also holds the Jardin botanique de Lyon and a small free zoo, and boats go out on the lake in summer.

The view works because it is so open. From the Île du Souvenir, in the north part of the lake, you look back across the water to the park's tree line and the north shore behind it. The water gives a calm foreground, and the trees give a soft green band across the middle of the picture. It suits a wide, relaxed photo that shows the scale of the park.

If you have time for a second picture, the ornate gilded gate called the Porte des Enfants du Rhône is worth a look. It is 32 metres long, and its central opening is 11 metres high. It was designed by Charles Meysson after a competition in 1898, and it frames the entrance well, often with the bronze centaur group and the park beyond. The glasshouse facade of the Grandes Serres, with plants and a statue in front, makes a third option. Weekend afternoons get busy, so an early visit gives you cleaner shots.
text.geographic_location: In the northern part of Lyon's 6th arrondissement, inside the large Parc de la Tête d'Or beside the Rhône.
text.directions_text: From central Lyon head north to the 6th arrondissement by taxi or hired scooter and go in through the park gates. The Île du Souvenir is reached on foot inside the park. Check the signs in the park for the current route to the island. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole lake and the tree line in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out a section of the far shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (north part of the lake, looking back across the water). The lake with the park's tree line and the north shore behind it, a wide classic panorama of the park. In the north part of the lake, and look back across the water. You should see the lake, the park's tree line and the north shore behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower line, so the horizon stays level and the trees fill the middle band. Leave some water in the foreground. A second option for another frame is the Porte des Enfants du Rhône, or the glasshouse facade of the Grandes Serres with plants and a statue in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the far tree line to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich. Try panorama mode for an extra-wide sweep, and move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early, as weekend afternoons are crowded. The rose garden is at its best in late spring to early summer, if you add it to your visit.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is inside a public park, reached on foot, but access rules for the island itself may vary, and some greenhouse areas may restrict photography, so check the official site and the signs on the day before you go.

name: Vieux Lyon
label: Vieux Lyon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Passerelle Saint-Vincent' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Passerelle Saint-Vincent' (way/242802641): middle (81 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/236823541: large area 'Historic Site of Lyon' (3479 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Renaissance old town with narrow streets and colourful facades.

text.description:
Vieux Lyon is the old Renaissance heart of the city, packed between the Saône and the Fourvière hill. It covers 24 hectares and is one of Europe's most extensive Renaissance neighbourhoods. It became the first site in France protected under the Malraux law in 1964, and it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998. It has three parts, Saint-Jean, Saint-Paul and Saint-Georges, each with its own character.

The best way to take it in on a phone is from the Passerelle Saint-Vincent, the footbridge over the Saône. From the middle of the bridge you see the pastel Renaissance facades lined up along the water, with the hill rising steeply behind them. The river gives you a clear gap in front of the buildings, so you can get the whole district in one frame. After dark the lights reflect on the water and the view becomes especially atmospheric.

For a second view, the Esplanade de Fourvière gives a wide panorama over the rooftops and the Saint-Jean cathedral. Place Saint-Jean is good for the cathedral front and the old square.

Keep to public space. Please don't photograph inside residential courtyards or the traboules (the passages through buildings) without permission, and don't block the narrow footbridge while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Vieux Lyon lies between the Fourvière hill and the river Saône, in the oldest part of the city. The Passerelle Saint-Vincent is the footbridge over the Saône that looks across to it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Lyon and walk to the Saône riverbank at the Passerelle Saint-Vincent. From there the subject is about 630 m to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the line of facades with the hill behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and hill, and keep the horizon level so the buildings don't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooflines, colours and the slope of Fourvière.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Passerelle Saint-Vincent (footbridge over the Saône, looking toward Vieux Lyon). The pastel Renaissance facades of Vieux Lyon along the Saône, with the Fourvière hill rising behind them. Face Vieux Lyon, with the old town to the south. The pastel Renaissance facades run along the water and Fourvière rises behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the line of facades along the lower third, with the hill filling the upper part. Include a strip of river in the foreground for depth. If the footbridge is busy, step to the side so you don't block people. For a different angle, try the Esplanade de Fourvière for the rooftops or Place Saint-Jean for the cathedral front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facades to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold your elbows against the parapet or your body to keep the lights on the water sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the lights reflect on the water and the view is at its most atmospheric. Dusk also works well, as the sky still has colour and the lights are coming on.

text.access_note: The footbridge and riverside are open public space, but the cathedral, museums and any courtyards have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Musée des Confluences
label: Musée des Confluences
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Berges du Rhône' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Berges du Rhône nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/440270631: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musée des Confluences' (188 m across).
notes: Deconstructivist science museum at the meeting of the Rhône and Saône.

text.description: The Musée des Confluences sits at the southern tip of the Presqu'île, where the Rhône and the Saône meet. It opened on 20 December 2014 as a science centre and anthropology museum. The building was designed by the Austrian firm Coop Himmelb(l)au in a deconstructivist style, and it is often compared to a floating cloud of stainless steel and glass. It stands 44 m high, 150 m long and 83 m wide, so it is a big, angular shape that fills a frame well. From the riverbank directly opposite, the museum can be reflected in the Rhône, with the Raymond Barre footbridge at the edge of the picture. This quieter stretch of path makes a calmer alternative to shooting from the bridge itself. Give yourself a little room at the edge of the frame so the footbridge adds depth rather than clutter. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the water line stays straight, because a tilted horizon spoils a reflection. If you want a different view, the Pont Raymond Barre shows the museum's whole silhouette with the hills behind it. The museum's own rooftop terrace is inside the building, so it is not a free outdoor spot.
text.geographic_location: In the Confluence quarter at the southern tip of Lyon's Presqu'île, in the 2nd arrondissement, beside the meeting of the Rhône and the Saône. The photo is taken from the Rhône's opposite bank, looking back at the museum.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Confluence quarter at the southern end of the Presqu'île and make your way on foot to the riverbank on the Rhône opposite the museum. The museum lies about 786 m to the south-west of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the museum, its reflection and the footbridge together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and the building will not fit. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the angular roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Berges du Rhône (riverbank on the Rhône, directly opposite the museum). The museum reflected in the river, with the Raymond Barre footbridge at the edge of the frame. Look south-west across the river and you should see the museum reflected in the Rhône, with the Raymond Barre footbridge at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the museum a little off-centre and let its reflection fill the lower half of the picture. Use the gridlines to keep the water line level, and keep the footbridge at one edge. For the museum's full silhouette against the hills, the Pont Raymond Barre is a good alternative. At night, the Pont de la Mulatière shows the lit museum near the confluence.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the bright glass is not washed out. In low light use night mode, and rest your phone against a railing or brace your elbows to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset or before sunrise, when the sky is deep blue and the museum's lights show in the water.

text.access_note: The riverbank path is an open public space, but the museum itself and its rooftop terrace are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Place des Terreaux
label: Place des Terreaux
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin du musée des Beaux-Arts' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/5117443: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place des Terreaux' (121 m across).
notes: Elegant square between the town hall and the fine arts museum.

text.description:
Place des Terreaux is the big open square in the middle of Lyon's Presqu'île, at the foot of the Croix-Rousse hill. It is framed by two grand buildings: the baroque Hôtel de Ville on the east side and the Musée des Beaux-Arts, in the former Palais Saint-Pierre, on the south side. The whole area is part of Lyon's UNESCO World Heritage zone. The square photographs well because so much sits within a few steps of each other: pale stone facades, a large bronze fountain, and a paved floor dotted with small water jets.

The fountain is the centrepiece. Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi made it, and it was unveiled here on 22 September 1891. It shows a woman driving a four-horse chariot. It was first made for Bordeaux, and Lyon bought it in 1890. The Hôtel de Ville was built between 1646 and 1651 and rebuilt after a fire in 1674. The museum building began as a convent and became a museum in 1803.

For a calmer take, try the museum's garden or courtyard, just beside the square. From there the museum's architecture is framed away from the traffic and the crowds around the fountain. Come back out afterwards for the fountain with the Hôtel de Ville behind it. The fountain area is busiest around midday, so early morning or late afternoon is usually more relaxed for photos.
text.geographic_location: Place des Terreaux is in the 1st arrondissement of Lyon, on the Presqu'île between the Rhône and the Saône, at the foot of the Croix-Rousse slopes. It sits between the Hôtel de Ville and the Musée des Beaux-Arts.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Presqu'île in the centre of Lyon and ask for Place des Terreaux, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. From there the square's centre is about 1 minute on foot to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the museum garden. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you move into the square for the fountain and the Hôtel de Ville together. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the horses of the chariot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardin du musée des Beaux-Arts (Within the museum grounds beside the square.). The museum's architecture framed from its garden or courtyard, away from the traffic and crowds of the open square. From here you frame the museum's architecture from its garden or courtyard, away from the traffic and crowds of the open square. The square itself lies just to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the museum's facade with the grid so the vertical lines stay straight. Leave a little space around the building rather than cropping tight. Once you are out in the square, the Bartholdi fountain makes a good foreground with the Hôtel de Ville behind it. That is a good second photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the pale stone keeps its detail. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls, and switch off the ultra-wide if the building edges look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the fountain area is quieter than at midday.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but check the official site for the museum garden's opening hours and entry rules before you go.

name: Lyon Cathedral
label: Saint-Jean Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Saint-Jean' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Saint-Jean' (way/35018432): middle (131 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/136200148: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathédrale Saint-Jean' (113 m across).
notes: Gothic cathedral in the old town with an astronomical clock.

text.description:
Lyon Cathedral, the Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist, stands on Place Saint-Jean in the old part of the city. Work began in 1180 and finished in 1476. Its west front is Gothic, while the apse and choir behind are Romanesque. In 1998 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List along with other historic sites in central Lyon.

It photographs well because the square gives you a clear, straight-on view of the façade and its rose window. The old Renaissance houses of Vieux Lyon sit around it and add colour and a sense of place. Moving between the corners of the square lets you vary the angle without leaving the spot. Inside, the 14th-century astronomical clock is one of the sights, but interior photography is limited to personal use and there are dress and security rules.

Each December the Festival of Lights puts a choreographed lighting display on the façade. The cathedral is also lit at twilight, which makes a good second visit if you came by day. In daylight the carved detail on the front is easiest to see, so it is worth zooming in on small areas as well as taking the full-width shot.

The square is fairly enclosed, so expect to tilt your phone upwards. Keep an eye on the gridlines to stop the towers leaning, and take a few frames from different corners before you move on.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is on Place Saint-Jean in central Lyon, in the old quarter of Vieux Lyon. It stands beside the Saône in Vieux Lyon.
text.directions_text: Head for Place Saint-Jean in Vieux Lyon. From there the west façade is straight ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade and the surrounding houses from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and the carved detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Saint-Jean (in front of the west façade, from the corners of the square). The cathedral's Gothic west façade and rose window filling the frame, with the old Renaissance houses of Vieux Lyon around it. From here the cathedral is to the east and the Gothic façade and rose window fill the frame, with the Renaissance houses of Vieux Lyon around it. Try the different corners of the square for varied angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines, keeping the phone as level as you can so the building does not lean back. Take one wide frame with the surrounding houses, then a tighter one on the rose window. For a very different view, the esplanade of the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière is higher up and shows the cathedral in the middle distance beside the Saône.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. At twilight, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In daytime the sunlight picks out the detail of the façade. At twilight, when the cathedral is lit, the front looks very different, and in December the Festival of Lights adds a lighting display.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship with dress and security rules and limits on interior photography, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Pointing a phone upwards at a tall façade makes the vertical lines lean, which the gridlines help correct.
The square is fairly enclosed, so the ultra-wide lens helps fit the whole façade in from close up.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in stonework against a bright sky.
Bracing your elbows helps steady a phone in night mode.

name: Museum of Fine Arts of Lyon
label: Fine Arts Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Terreaux' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Terreaux' (way/5117443): middle (120 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/493540665: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon' (162 m across).
notes: Large art museum in a former abbey, with a quiet cloister garden.

text.description:
The Museum of Fine Arts of Lyon fills a former Benedictine convent, the Royal Abbey of Saint-Pierre-les-Nonnains, built in the 17th century and remodelled under Louis XIV. That history is why the front looks more like a grand abbey than a gallery. The museum sits on Place des Terreaux, and the open square gives you the space to step back and fit the whole façade into one frame. Behind the walls are collections running from ancient Egypt to modern art, and it is counted among the largest art museums in France.

The best outdoor photo is the straight-on view from the square, with the abbey-style front across the open space and the surrounding Terreaux buildings closing in on either side. Behind the façade, the old cloister is now a quiet garden in the middle of the city, with statues (including two by Rodin) among arches and greenery. It makes a good second photo if you go in. The museum was restored between 1988 and 1998 and stayed open to visitors throughout.

Keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight, and use the gridlines to line up the façade. Allow a little time for people crossing the square; a short wait usually gives you a clearer frame.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Lyon, on the peninsula, right beside Place des Terreaux. The museum fills the former abbey buildings on the square.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so head for Place des Terreaux in the centre of the peninsula. Stand on the square, just north of the museum, and face south toward the main façade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole façade across the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand close and the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved stonework, windows and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Terreaux (east side of the square, facing the museum's main façade). The abbey-style front of the museum across the open square, framed by the surrounding Terreaux buildings. From here you see the abbey-style front across the open square, framed by the surrounding Terreaux buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the façade and use the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Leave some open square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Telephoto is good for architectural details. If you go inside, the Jardin du musée des Beaux-Arts is a second option, with sculptures and arches framed by the stone arcades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames while people cross the square and choose the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and late afternoon often gives softer light on the stone. Check how the shadows fall on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the museum and its garden follow the museum's own opening hours, so check the official site before you go, including whether photography is allowed.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning on the square is usually quieter than later in the day.
Late afternoon often gives softer light on the façade, though the exact light depends on the day and season.
Place des Terreaux is an open public square that can be entered freely.
Pedestrians crossing the square may briefly get in the frame.

name: Mur des Canuts
label: Mur des Canuts
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Boulevard des Canuts' (6 web pages); placed at crossing of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W251734547 (Mur des Canuts): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Giant trompe-l'oeil mural in the Croix-Rousse district.

text.description:
The Mur des Canuts is a huge painted wall at the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau. It looks like a real street scene, with a staircase climbing between tall buildings, but it is all paint on the side of an ordinary residential building.

The angle matters. Reviewers say the illusion works best from across the road, standing diagonally from the wall, rather than straight on. Guides also point to this corner as the one place where the perspective reads properly. From there you can fit the whole facade, the staircase and the painted street life into one frame.

Guides say the wall has been repainted in 1987, 1997 and 2013, so details may differ from older photos you have seen. Midday sun is said to flatten the painted staircase, so aim for the morning if you can.

For your photo, cross the road, turn to face the wall and take a few steps along the pavement until the staircase looks as if it recedes. Take one shot with the whole wall in view, then a closer one of a detail, such as a window or a figure. Keep clear of the doorways and watch the traffic on the boulevard while you line things up.
text.geographic_location: On the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau, Lyon.
text.directions_text: Head for the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives the most natural-looking perspective on the painted staircase. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole wall in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the wall's edges parallel to the sides of the screen so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau (across the road, standing diagonally from the wall at the corner). The whole painted facade, with the staircase climbing between the tall painted buildings and the trompe-l'oeil street scene in one frame. The wall is to the south of you. From here the whole painted facade, the staircase between the tall painted buildings and the trompe-l'oeil street scene fit in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the painted buildings with them. Include the whole wall first, then try a tighter shot of one detail using 2x if your phone has it. Moving a few steps along the pavement changes how the staircase seems to recede, so check a couple of positions on screen.

name: Opéra de Lyon
label: Opéra de Lyon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de la Comédie' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place de la Comédie' (way/133953059): middle (60 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/10061086: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Opéra de Lyon' (76 m across).
notes: Neoclassical opera house with a modern glass dome by Jean Nouvel.

text.description: The Opéra de Lyon is an opera house with two faces. The front is a 19th-century neo-classical façade with arcades and eight statues of the muses. Behind and above it sits a modern steel-and-glass barrel vault. The first opera house, the Grand Théâtre, opened in Lyon in 1756 and was designed by Jacques-Germain Soufflot. The present building opened on 1 July 1831. Between 1985 and 1993 the architect Jean Nouvel rebuilt the inside. He kept only the foyer and the outer façade, dug down for rehearsal space and doubled the building's height with the glass vault. That mix of old stone and new glass is what makes it a good photo subject. The Hôtel de Ville stands across the square, which gives you a second grand building to play with. Stand back far enough to fit the arcades and the statues along the top, then check that the building looks straight on your screen. If you want a closer picture, zoom in on the statues rather than walking up to the doors. For a different view, the Esplanade de Fourvière shows the glass roof among the city's rooftops, and Pont Morand may give a view of the opera across the Rhône, but check this on the ground.
text.geographic_location: The opera stands in central Lyon, on Place de la Comédie, directly opposite the Hôtel de Ville.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Place de la Comédie in central Lyon. The Hôtel de Ville is on the far side of the square, and the opera is the building facing it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the arcades, the muse statues and some of the square in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural look. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and the glass vault above.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de la Comédie (in front of the main facade, facing the Hôtel de Ville across the square). The full neo-classical front of the opera with its arcades and eight muse statues, with the Hôtel de Ville visible across the square. From here you see the full neo-classical front of the opera, with its arcades and eight muse statues. The Hôtel de Ville is across the square, behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so the columns don't lean. Keep your phone level. Fitting the whole front in at 0.5x will tilt the edges slightly, so leave a little space around the building and crop afterwards. For an alternative, try the Esplanade de Fourvière for a distant view of the glass roof among the red rooftops. Pont Morand may give a view of the opera across the Rhône, but check this on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. As the light fades, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or dusk, when the statues and arcades are lit.

text.access_note: Place de la Comédie is an open pedestrian square, free to photograph from, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, and note that flash and recording are not allowed during performances.

name: Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière
label: Fourvière Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place Saint-Jean' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Saint-Jean' (way/35018432): middle (131 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29179429: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière' (83 m across).
notes: White basilica on the hill above the old town.

text.description:
The white basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière sits on top of its hill and can be seen from many parts of Lyon, which is why it has become the city's symbol. It was built between 1872 and 1896, on ground that was once the Roman forum of Trajan. The architect, Pierre Bossan, drew on Romanesque and Byzantine styles. The result has four main towers and a bell tower topped with a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary. Locals call it "the upside-down elephant", and once you have seen the four tower 'legs' it is hard to unsee.

For a phone photo, the classic composition is from Place Saint-Jean in Vieux Lyon. From there the basilica rises above the old rooftops and facades, so you get the old town and the hilltop church in one frame. The pale stone stands out well against a blue sky, and the warm old buildings in the foreground give the picture depth. Keep the basilica in the upper part of the frame and let the rooftops fill the rest.

If you want a different view, the Esplanade de Fourvière up the hill is better for the city skyline, with the basilica behind you. The Jardin du Rosaire is a quieter spot with views across Lyon.
text.geographic_location: The basilica stands on Fourvière hill, above Vieux Lyon.
text.directions_text: Head for Vieux Lyon and Place Saint-Jean, the old-town square at the foot of the hill. Once in the square, the basilica is up the hill to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the basilica and the rooftops sit together in one frame. If the basilica looks small, try the telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring it closer and squeeze the view of hill and roofs together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the old facades in the square, as it will make the basilica tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place Saint-Jean (Vieux Lyon side, facing up the hill to the basilica). The white basilica rising above the rooftops and old facades of Vieux Lyon, the classic 'basilica over the old town' composition. From here the white basilica rises above the rooftops and old facades of Vieux Lyon, the classic 'basilica over the old town' view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the basilica on the upper line, with the rooftops and facades filling the lower two-thirds. Keep the phone level so the old buildings don't lean. For a different view, the Esplanade de Fourvière gives the city skyline, with the basilica behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the basilica to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stone keeps its detail against the bright sky. Check that people in the square are not walking into the frame before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the sky before you go, because a clear day suits the white stone.

text.access_note: The basilica is a place of worship with guided tours and a museum, and access to the north tower is only at certain times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The basilica's pale stone stands out against a clear blue sky.

name: Hôtel de Ville, Lyon
label: Hôtel de Ville
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Terreaux' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Terreaux' (way/5117443): middle (120 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1221535523: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hôtel de ville' (140 m across).
notes: 17th-century town hall facing Place des Terreaux.

text.description: Lyon's Hôtel de Ville is the city hall, and it is one of the largest historic buildings in town. It stands between the Place des Terreaux and the Place de la Comédie, facing the opera house. The classic photo is taken from the Place des Terreaux. Frame the Bartholdi Fountain in the foreground, with the long stone front of the city hall rising behind it. The front is symmetrical, with nine bays and a pavilion at each end, so a straight-on shot looks tidy and balanced. Building work began on 5 September 1646, timed to King Louis XIV's birthday, and the council first met here in 1652. A fire in 1674 led to the façade being restored and altered. The belfry was added to the UNESCO World Heritage group of Belfries of Belgium and France in 2005. Look up at the roofline and the clock tower with its dome, and at the half-relief in the middle of the façade, which shows King Henry IV on horseback. The building is also lit up well after dark, so dusk and evening are good times to come. If you want more of the ornate detail, walk round to the Place de la Comédie. From there you can take the east façade in one frame. The interior is not normally open to visitors, so plan on photographing from outside.
text.geographic_location: In the Presqu'île, the central peninsula of Lyon, between the Place des Terreaux and the Place de la Comédie. It sits right in front of the opera house.
text.directions_text: The Place des Terreaux and the Place de la Comédie are both served by the Hôtel de Ville metro stop on line A, so get off there. From there the building is about 2 minutes on foot to the east, and its façade faces you across the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the fountain and the whole façade in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. A telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for the clock tower and the half-relief on the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Terreaux (in front of the building, with the Bartholdi Fountain in the foreground). The classic postcard frame: the fountain in the foreground with the city hall's facade behind it. In front of the building, with the Bartholdi Fountain in the foreground. From here you get the classic postcard frame, with the fountain in front and the city hall's façade behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the façade up with them so the verticals stay straight. Put the fountain in the lower part of the frame and let the building fill the rest. For an alternative, try the Place de la Comédie, which shows the east façade in one frame and catches more of its ornate detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit façade is not washed out against the dark sky. After dark, use night mode and brace your phone against something solid, or hold it steady with both hands, so the lights stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or evening, when the building is illuminated.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the city hall interior is not normally open to visitors, so check the official site before you go for any event closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The Hôtel de Ville metro stop on line A is at or right beside the Place des Terreaux.
Keeping gridlines on helps keep the façade's vertical lines straight.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop a lit façade looking washed out against a dark sky.

name: Place des Jacobins
label: Place des Jacobins
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Jacobins' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Jacobins' (relation/4218607): middle (85 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3464806: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place des Jacobins' (118 m across).
notes: Square with a large ornate fountain.

text.description:
Place des Jacobins is a broad, busy square in the middle of Lyon's 2nd arrondissement, and its centrepiece is the white marble Fontaine des Jacobins. The square dates back to 1556. It takes its name from the Dominican friars, known as Jacobins, who had a convent here from 1296. The fountain you see today was inaugurated on 14 July 1885. It was designed by Gaspard André and is topped by four statues of artists: Flandrin, Audran, Coustou and Philibert de l'Orme. Twelve streets lead into the square, and the whole area lies within the UNESCO World Heritage zone.

It photographs well because the fountain stands in the open, with the 19th-century facades surrounding the square and forming the backdrop. Stand in front of the fountain, near the centre of the square, and you can fit the white stonework and the facades into one frame. If you have time, try a second angle from Rue Mercière, where the central statues line up neatly with the square. The square can be crowded at peak times and on market days, so an early or quiet visit gives you cleaner pictures. Watch for traffic and passers-by at the edges of the frame.
text.geographic_location: Place des Jacobins sits in the centre of Lyon's 2nd arrondissement, where a dozen streets meet around the fountain. Rue Mercière and Rue Émile Zola are nearby streets that give other views of the fountain.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head on foot for the centre of the 2nd arrondissement and look for Place des Jacobins. The square is a meeting point for twelve streets, so you can reach it from several directions. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the facades behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the basin and the surrounding facades. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Jacobins (in front of the fountain, near the centre of the square). The white marble Fontaine des Jacobins framed by the 19th-century facades that surround the square. The middle of the square lies just to the west. From here the white marble fountain is framed by the 19th-century facades around the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and keep the fountain's central statues on the middle line, so the facades sit level behind it. For a symmetrical alternative, walk to Rue Mercière and shoot straight at the fountain. From Rue Émile Zola, use the basin edge in the foreground to lead the eye back to the ornate buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the marble keeps its detail and does not turn pure white. In the evening, when the fountain and buildings are lit, hold the phone steady against your body or a solid ledge. Use night mode only if the scene looks dim, and keep still while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour or evening, when the fountain and buildings are lit, is the favourite time. Early morning also suits the carvings and is usually quieter, though the best light can vary, so check on the day.

text.access_note: This is an open public square, but professional shoots may need permits, so check permit rules before a professional shoot.

name: Ancient Theatre of Fourvière
label: Roman Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Théâtre antique de Fourvière' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/88526502: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Théâtre Gallo-Romain de Fourvière' (143 m across).
notes: Roman theatre from 15 BC with views over the city.

text.description:
The Ancient Theatre of Fourvière is a Roman theatre built on the hill of Fourvière, in the middle of what was the Roman city of Lyon. The first theatre went up around 15 BC. In the early 2nd century it was enlarged to a diameter of about 108 m, with room for some 10,000 people. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the historic centre of Lyon. It is still used today, and the Nuits de Fourvière festival is held here every year.

It photographs well because of its shape. The stone seating sweeps round in a big curve, and from the upper tiers the city of Lyon spreads out behind it. That gives you ancient stone in the foreground and a modern skyline beyond, all in one frame. The phone icon on the map is on the upper tiers of the seating, where the wide curve below you and the city behind both fit in one shot.

Take your time on the steps and look for repeating lines: the curved rows of stone make natural leading lines towards the centre. For a different picture, turn round and shoot the tiers rising above you, which shows the height and scale of the seating. Another wide view of the whole semicircle, with the Odéon and the city beyond, is possible from the terrace of the Musée gallo-romain de Fourvière. Check the official site before you go, as that terrace may need museum access.
text.geographic_location: The theatre stands on the hill of Fourvière, in the historic centre of Lyon, on the site of the old Roman city. It sits close to the Musée gallo-romain de Fourvière.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or funicular stop is listed for this spot, so check the official site for the best way up to the hill of Fourvière. Once you are at the theatre, climb the seating to the upper tiers, where the phone icon on the map is. Follow the signs on site and check the official site before you go for the best way in on the day. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curve of seating and the city behind it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the stone steps or a single row of tiers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the upper tiers of the seating at the Théâtre antique de Fourvière. From there you look down over the full curve of stone seating, with the city of Lyon spread out behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the curved rows along the lower third of the frame, with the city filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the steps don't lean. For a closer, more dramatic shot, point up at the tiers rising above you to show their height. A second wide view of the whole semicircle is possible from the Musée gallo-romain terrace, if it is open.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out and the stone keeps its colour. Keep your elbows tucked in for a steadier shot, and use panorama only if you can sweep slowly and evenly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, when the low light warms the stone and the city behind it.

text.access_note: The theatre itself is understood to be free to enter, but the museum terrace may need museum access, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: The Halles de Lyon-Paul Bocuse is a covered food market in Lyon. It should suit a phone photographer because the subject can change every few steps. Outside, you can take a straightforward picture of the building. Inside, look for food stalls and counters. Lighting can vary from place to place, so check how it looks on your screen and adjust as you go. If the market is busy, people will walk through your frame. Treat that as part of the picture, since market photos often work best with a little life in them. For the building itself, use the gridlines to keep the edges straight. Then go in and take one wide shot to show the scale of the hall, followed by a few close pictures of single stalls or dishes. Use portrait mode for food on a counter, and ask before photographing a stallholder up close. Photography rules and opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Halles de Lyon-Paul Bocuse is in Lyon.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to reach the market. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

name: Fontaine Bartholdi
label: Bartholdi Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Terreaux' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Terreaux' (way/5117443): middle (120 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/55071957: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fontaine Bartholdi' (28 m across).
notes: Monumental fountain with four horses by Bartholdi.

text.description: The Fontaine Bartholdi is a huge bronze-looking fountain on Place des Terreaux, in the 1st arrondissement, and it is one of the easiest subjects in Lyon to photograph. France, shown as a woman, sits on a chariot pulled by four wildly rearing horses. They stand for the four great rivers of France, and their reins are made of water weeds. Bartholdi, the sculptor who made the Statue of Liberty, designed it. It was built in 1889 and put up on this square in September 1892. It is actually made of lead on an iron frame and weighs about 21 tons. It has been a protected historic monument since 1995. After restoration work that began in 2016, it was inaugurated again in March 2018, with water running and lighting. It photographs well because the horses and spray give you movement and drama, and the tall façades around the square make a natural frame. The fountain is large, so step back a little if you want the full group. Earlier visitors have found scaffolding, fencing or an empty basin during works, so check current conditions before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the 1st arrondissement of Lyon, on Place des Terreaux in the heart of the Presqu'île, opposite the Musée des Beaux-Arts and with the Hôtel de Ville on the square's other side.
text.directions_text: There are no metro or tram stops at this spot, so head for the 1st arrondissement on the Presqu'île and reach Place des Terreaux on foot. The fountain is directly north of you, so you will be facing it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole chariot and horses. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the fountain doesn't fit, or if you want the surrounding façades in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the horses' heads and the spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Terreaux (front of the fountain, facing the Hôtel de Ville side). The full bronze chariot and four rearing horses with spraying water, framed by the tall façades around the square. From here you can see the full chariot and the four rearing horses with the water spraying, framed by the tall façades around the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the chariot in the centre, keeping the horizon line level so the façades stay straight. Keep the phone level, as tilting it up makes the buildings lean inwards. For a wider view with more of the square around the fountain, an alternative is Place des Jacobins, which shows the fountain together with the façades and a sense of the space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the horses to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright spray and sky don't wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving water. If the fountain is lit after dark, use night mode and hold the phone as steady as you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people in front of the fountain. In the evening, the lit fountain gives a different mood, so try both if you can.

text.access_note: It stands in an open public square, free to see, but check current conditions before you go, as works have sometimes put up fencing or scaffolding.

name: Basilica of Saint-Martin d'Ainay
label: Ainay Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue Claude Bourgelat' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Rue Bourgelat' (roads).

notes: Romanesque basilica in the Ainay quarter.

text.description: Basilica of Saint-Martin d'Ainay is a Romanesque church in the Ainay area of Lyon's Presqu'île, inside the historic centre that is on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The abbey church was built at the end of the 11th century and consecrated on 29 January 1107. It was raised to the rank of basilica in 1905. It photographs well because the old stonework still looks solid and sturdy. The building was apparently designed with defence in mind, with massive walls, narrow window openings and a watchtower. Despite many changes over the centuries, including a 19th-century Romanesque Revival restoration that added side chapels, the church keeps a real unity of style. Inside, the nave is 17 metres wide and the whole building is 37 metres long. From the street you can usually frame much of the exterior, depending on how close you stand. From Rue Claude Bourgelat you see the basilica from the street, with the church sitting among the buildings of the neighbourhood. This gives a feel of the place rather than an isolated monument shot. If you want a different angle, try Place d'Ainay, where the church stands in its own square and you see it from the south-east. Keep the phone level so the walls and tower do not lean. Take a few frames at different zoom levels and pick the one that feels most balanced. The church is still in use for worship, so be considerate if anything is going on.
text.geographic_location: The basilica stands in Ainay, in the Presqu'île district of Lyon's historic centre. Rue Claude Bourgelat is the street beside it, and Place d'Ainay is nearby.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so the area is best reached on foot. Place d'Ainay is close by if you want a second angle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the church from the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the tower and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue Claude Bourgelat. The basilica's exterior seen from the street, the view that Wikimedia Commons and Wikidata use for the church. From here the photo shows the basilica's exterior seen from the street, with the church to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them so the walls do not lean. Keep the phone upright and avoid tilting it upwards, or the tower will lean back. Leave a little space around the building so it sits within the street scene. For a different view, walk to Place d'Ainay, where the church is set in its own square and seen from the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames at 0.5x, 1x and a gentle zoom, then choose the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter old stone. Early in the day usually means fewer people and cars in the frame.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but the basilica is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go and ask or check before photographing inside, especially during services.

label: Cour des Voraces
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'rue Imbert-Colomès' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of rue Imbert-Colomès nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/197673569: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cour des Voraces' (23 m across).
notes: Famous Croix-Rousse courtyard with a huge open staircase.

text.description:
The Cour des Voraces is a courtyard building on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse, in the Pentes quarter of Lyon's 1st arrondissement. It is best known for its huge six-floor stone stairway. You reach it through a traboule, one of Lyon's covered passages, which makes the visit feel like stepping out of the street and into a different world. The building dates from 1840 and is a good example of the canuts' architecture. The canuts were the silk weavers who shaped this neighbourhood. A plaque on the building recalls their struggle for their lives and dignity. The name comes from the Voraces, weavers known for their republican uprisings of 1848 and 1849. The court is also often mentioned as a symbol of resistance in the Second World War. Today it is social housing, and the court and its two staircases are classified as a historic monument.

It photographs well because of its repeating lines: stacked landings, wrought-iron railings and stone steps. From the street, the arched entrance gives a first frame of the way in. Inside, the stairs reward a look both up and down. Because people live here, keep your voice low, do not block the doors and do not photograph residents. Take a few frames in each spot, then move on.
text.geographic_location: In the Pentes quarter on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse, in Lyon's 1st arrondissement. The passage links Place Colbert, Montée Saint-Sébastien and rue Imbert-Colomès.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Pentes de la Croix-Rousse area of the 1st arrondissement and reach the entrance on foot. The entrance on rue Imbert-Colomès is at no. 29. The other entrances are at 9 Place Colbert and 14 bis Montée Saint-Sébastien. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) at the entrance for the arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) once inside, to fit the tall stairwell into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on rue Imbert-Colomès (at the traboule entrance from the street). The arched passage entrance from the street, framing the way into the courtyard. Where the traboule meets the street. From here the photo shows the arched passage entrance framing the way into the courtyard. It is a less obvious approach than the Place Colbert door, giving a different view of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the vertical lines so the walls stay straight. Keep the arch as a dark frame around the brighter courtyard beyond. Inside, the full height of the six-storey staircase with its wrought-iron railings is the other classic view. The courtyard and stairs seen falling away from above is a third, if you are allowed up. Take the ultra-wide (0.5x) shot from low down, with the phone held level so the lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the courtyard to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky and walls don't wash out. If the passage is dim, hold the phone steady against a wall and let night mode work for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight gives the most light inside the court. Opening hours are not confirmed, so check access locally before you plan a visit around any particular time.

text.access_note: This is a passage through an inhabited building. Opening hours and photo restrictions are not confirmed, so check access locally before going in.

name: Tour Incity
label: Incity Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanade de Fourvière' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Esplanade de Fourvière' (way/60752857): middle (101 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/368018684: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tour Incity' (53 m across).
notes: Tall modern skyscraper in the Part-Dieu business district.

text.description:
Tour Incity is the tallest building in the Greater Lyon area, at 200 m with 39 floors. It was built between 2013 and 2015 in the La Part-Dieu business district, on the site of the old UAP tower. The top is shaped to look symmetrical from wherever you see it in the city, which suits distant photos. Lights at the summit are also used to show the next day's air quality, shading from blue to mauve.

From the Esplanade de Fourvière, the tower is best treated as part of the skyline rather than the main subject. It rises as a silhouette above the red rooftops of Vieux Lyon, with the city spread out below. The tower is small in the frame from here, so zoom in and keep the rooftops in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Blue hour, just after sunset, is the best moment, when the city lights come on against the dark sky.

If you want a different angle, the Jardin des Chartreux is suggested for sunset reflections on the tower's glass. Le Jardin Suspendu is suggested for a view where Le Crayon is reflected in the facade. The tower is an office building, so this is a photo to take from a distance rather than a place to visit.
text.geographic_location: Tour Incity stands in the La Part-Dieu district of Lyon, at the corner of Rue Garibaldi and Cours Lafayette. The viewpoint is the Esplanade de Fourvière, the hilltop terrace above Vieux Lyon.
text.directions_text: The tower is in the La Part-Dieu district, and the Esplanade de Fourvière is on the hill about 2 km to its west. On foot it is a long walk, and the last stretch climbs. You can also use the funicular up the hill; check the official site for details before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (3x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower itself. Switch to the default lens (1x) or ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wider city view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Esplanade de Fourvière. Tour Incity rises as a silhouette above the red rooftops of Vieux Lyon, with the city spread out below. The tower rises as a silhouette above the red rooftops of Vieux Lyon, with the city spread out below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines. Leave a band of red rooftops along the bottom to give the tower scale. If the esplanade is busy, shoot over the terrace edge rather than between people. For an alternative, try the Jardin des Chartreux for sunset on the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays deep and the city lights do not blow out. Brace your elbows on the terrace wall when zoomed in. At dusk, night mode with a steady hold helps.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset, when the city lights come on against the dark sky.

text.access_note: The Esplanade de Fourvière is an open public terrace and free to visit; the tower itself is an office building, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.
claims_not_in_sources: At this distance the tower looks small in the frame, so a 3x-5x telephoto helps.
The last part of the walk to the esplanade is uphill.
Gripping the phone against the terrace wall or with elbows tucked in reduces blur when zoomed.
The tower is an office building and not open for general visits.

name: Metallic tower of Fourvière
label: Fourvière Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanade de la Basilique Notre-Dame de Fourvière' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Basilique Notre-Dame de Fourvière' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/320879095: the OpenStreetMap point 'Tour métallique de Fourvière'.
notes: Mini Eiffel-style TV tower on Fourvière hill.

text.description:
The Metallic tower of Fourvière is a steel lattice tower on top of Lyon's Fourvière hill. It looks a lot like a smaller cousin of the Eiffel Tower, which is three years older. The tower was built between 1892 and 1894. It stands 101 m tall, or about 86 m before the television antenna was added, and weighs 210 tons. At 372 metres above sea level, it sits on the highest point in Lyon. It was once an observation tower, but it has been closed to visitors since 1953 and now works as a television mast, so every photo of it is taken from outside.

It photographs well because the pale basilica and the dark open ironwork sit very close together, with the city spread out below. From the esplanade in front of the basilica you can frame the tower rising behind and beside the church, with the skyline in the same shot. That gives you a sense of place in a single frame, which a close-up of the tower alone does not.

Keep the phone level, switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Leave some sky above the top of the mast, and watch for people and railings at the edges of the frame. If the esplanade is busy, the Passerelle des Quatre Vents footbridge gives a different view across the rooftops and trees, with the basilica close by.
text.geographic_location: The tower is on the Fourvière hill in Lyon, just beside the Notre-Dame de Fourvière basilica. The city lies spread out below it.
text.directions_text: Check a local map for the route up to the basilica esplanade. From the esplanade the tower is a short distance to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower, the basilica and the skyline together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the esplanade is crowded or you want more of the basilica. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the lattice against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Esplanade de la Basilique Notre-Dame de Fourvière (in front of the basilica, looking towards the tower). The tower rising behind and beside the basilica, with the city skyline spread below in the same frame. Face north and look towards the tower. It rises behind and beside the basilica, with the city skyline below in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the basilica on one side and the tower on the other, and keep the skyline in the lower part of the frame. Use the gridlines to keep the mast upright. For a different angle, try the Passerelle des Quatre Vents, which shows the tower across the rooftops and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the tower to set focus and exposure, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the steel keeps its detail. In dim light, hold the phone steady against a wall or railing and let night mode do its work.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is a good time, when the skyline and sky colour up behind the tower. During the Fête des Lumières the tower is lit up, which makes for striking evening shots.

text.access_note: The esplanade is an outdoor public square, but the tower itself is closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go for any event or restriction.
